claim: A membrane 'staple' consisting of membrane-anchored repeats of the trans-aggregating FM domain facing the lumen of the secretory pathway was designed.
source_text: We have designed a membrane 'staple', which consists of membrane-anchored repeats of the trans-aggregating FM domain that face the lumen of the secretory pathway.
evidence_reasoning: The design is described and its properties are demonstrated through experimental data; the functional behavior is inferred from the design principles.

claim: In the presence of disaggregating drug, FM domain-containing proteins transit the secretory pathway.
source_text: In the presence of the disaggregating drug these proteins transit the secretory pathway.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental observations showing protein movement through the secretory pathway when drug is present.

claim: When the disaggregating drug is removed, FM domain-containing proteins form electron-dense plaques termed staples.
source_text: When the drug is removed these proteins form electron-dense plaques which we term staples.
evidence_reasoning: Electron microscopy data directly shows the formation of electron-dense plaques upon drug removal.

claim: Membrane staples initially positioned within the cis-Golgi remained at the cis face of the Golgi even after many hours.
source_text: Unexpectedly, when initially positioned within the cis-Golgi, staples remained at the cis face of the Golgi even after many hours.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary experimental finding supported by multiple imaging and biochemical assays over extended time periods.

claim: Soluble FM-aggregates transit the Golgi.
source_text: By contrast, soluble FM-aggregates transited the Golgi.
evidence_reasoning: Experimental data shows movement of soluble aggregates through the Golgi stack.

claim: Membrane staples and soluble aggregates placed in cis-Golgi cisternae have different fates.
source_text: Staples and soluble aggregates placed in cis-Golgi cisternae therefore have different fates.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from comparative experimental data showing differential behavior of the two types of aggregates.

claim: Membrane staples are located in the flattened, stacked central regions of the cisternae.
source_text: Whereas the membrane staples are located in the flattened, stacked central regions of the cisternae, the soluble aggregates are in the dilated rims.
evidence_reasoning: Electron microscopy data directly shows the spatial distribution of staples in cisternal centers.

claim: Soluble aggregates are located in the dilated rims of cisternae.
source_text: Whereas the membrane staples are located in the flattened, stacked central regions of the cisternae, the soluble aggregates are in the dilated rims.
evidence_reasoning: Electron microscopy data shows the preferential localization of soluble aggregates to cisternal rims.

claim: Cisternae are static on the time scale of protein traffic.
source_text: This suggests that while the cisternae are static on the time scale of protein traffic, the dilated rims are mobile and progress in the cis → trans direction via a mechanism that we term 'Rim Progression'.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the observation that membrane staples remain in place while transport continues, supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Dilated rims are mobile and progress in the cis to trans direction via a mechanism termed 'Rim Progression'.
source_text: This suggests that while the cisternae are static on the time scale of protein traffic, the dilated rims are mobile and progress in the cis → trans direction via a mechanism that we term 'Rim Progression'.
evidence_reasoning: This mechanism is proposed based on the differential behavior of soluble aggregates (which move) versus membrane staples (which remain static).

claim: Anterograde transport through the Golgi stack is a prerequisite for virtually all proteins that are secreted, targeted to the cell surface, or localized in internal membrane-bound compartments in plants and animals.
source_text: Anterograde transport (cis → trans) through the Golgi stack is a prerequisite for virtually all proteins that are ultimately secreted from the cell, targeted to the cell surface membrane, or localized in a plethora of internal membrane-bound compartments in plants and animals.
evidence_reasoning: This is established scientific knowledge about the fundamental role of Golgi transport.

claim: The Golgi transport process was first recognized over 50 years ago.
source_text: Despite the fact that this fundamental process was first recognized over 50 years ago, there is still today no general agreement on how it works.
evidence_reasoning: This is a historical fact about the discovery of Golgi transport.

claim: There is no general agreement on how anterograde Golgi transport works.
source_text: Despite the fact that this fundamental process was first recognized over 50 years ago, there is still today no general agreement on how it works.
evidence_reasoning: This reflects the current state of scientific understanding and debate in the field.

claim: Golgi stacks typically comprise 4-6 cisternae.
source_text: The greatest distinction among the competing models for anterograde transport (reviewed in Rothman, 2010) is whether the 4–6 cisternae typically comprising the Golgi stack are proposed to be static or mobile over the time scale of protein flow across the Golgi (typically 5–20 min).
evidence_reasoning: This is established structural knowledge about Golgi organization.

claim: Protein flow across the Golgi typically takes 5-20 minutes.
source_text: The greatest distinction among the competing models for anterograde transport (reviewed in Rothman, 2010) is whether the 4–6 cisternae typically comprising the Golgi stack are proposed to be static or mobile over the time scale of protein flow across the Golgi (typically 5–20 min).
evidence_reasoning: This is established kinetic information about Golgi transport rates.

claim: In static models of Golgi transport, a transport process such as budding/fusing COPI transport vesicles or tubules is required to create anterograde flow of cargo.
source_text: In 'static' models, a transport process such as budding/fusing COPI transport vesicles or possibly tubules is required to create anterograde flow of cargo.
evidence_reasoning: This describes one of the competing theoretical models for Golgi transport.

claim: In mobile models of Golgi transport, cisternae continuously move as intact units in the cis to trans direction, forming at the cis face and being consumed at the trans face.
source_text: In contrast, in 'mobile' models, the cisternae themselves continuously move as intact units in the cis → trans direction (termed 'cisternal progression'), forming at the cis face and being consumed at the trans face, so that no inter-cisternal transport process is required in the anterograde direction.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the cisternal progression model, an alternative theoretical framework.

claim: Mobile/cisternal progression models require concomitant retrograde transport of Golgi resident enzymes, termed 'cisternal maturation'.
source_text: In order to allow the Golgi stack to retain its resident proteins (such as glycosyltransferases) in the face of continuous cisternal turnover, mobile/cisternal progression models also require concomitant retrograde transport (trans → cis or Golgi → ER, or both) of steady-state Golgi resident enzymes, termed 'cisternal maturation'
evidence_reasoning: This describes a theoretical requirement of the cisternal maturation model, supported by citations to Glick and colleagues.

claim: Intrinsically large soluble cargoes such as immature collagen aggregates are far too large to be accommodated by COPI transport vesicles.
source_text: The strongest evidence for cisternal progression in Golgi stacks is that intrinsically large soluble cargoes such as immature collagen aggregates (Bonfanti et al., 1998)—which are far too large to be accommodated by COPI transport vesicles—can nonetheless be rapidly transported across the stack.
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about the size constraints of COPI vesicles relative to collagen aggregates.

claim: Large soluble cargoes such as immature collagen aggregates can be rapidly transported across the Golgi stack.
source_text: The strongest evidence for cisternal progression in Golgi stacks is that intrinsically large soluble cargoes such as immature collagen aggregates (Bonfanti et al., 1998)—which are far too large to be accommodated by COPI transport vesicles—can nonetheless be rapidly transported across the stack.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by the cited work of Bonfanti et al., 1998.

claim: It has been widely accepted by deductive reasoning that whole cisternae must progress across the stack based on the transport of large collagen aggregates.
source_text: On this basis it has been widely accepted by deductive reasoning, as distinct from direct visualization, that whole cisternae must indeed progress across the stack.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the prevailing interpretation in the field based on indirect evidence.

claim: Parallel processes of COPI vesicular transport and/or tubule-based transport could occur alongside cisternal progression.
source_text: This of course does not rule out that parallel processes of COPI vesicular transport (Pelham and Rothman, 2000) and/or tubule-based transport (Trucco et al., 2004) could also occur.
evidence_reasoning: This acknowledges the possibility of multiple concurrent transport mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Cadherins consist of tandem repeats of an adhesive unit that binds itself preferentially in trans.
source_text: Cadherins consist of tandem repeats of an adhesive unit that binds itself preferentially in trans (Pokutta and Weis, 2007).
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about cadherin structure, supported by citation.

claim: The FKBP mutant termed FM interacts in trans according to its crystal packing.
source_text: A similar unit, which additionally is controllable with soluble ligands that can enter cells, is the FKBP mutant termed FM, which according to its crystal packing also interacts in trans (Rollins et al., 2000)
evidence_reasoning: This structural property is supported by the cited crystallographic study.

claim: FM domain trans-interaction is disrupted by ligands such as AP21998 even in living cells.
source_text: with the additional feature that this interaction is disrupted by ligands such as AP21998 even in living cells (Rivera et al., 2000).
evidence_reasoning: This functional property is supported by the cited work of Rivera et al.

claim: Tandem membrane-anchored repeats of FM domains should mimic cadherin in producing a defined structure that will reversibly adhere intracellular membranes.
source_text: This suggests that tandem membrane-anchored repeats of FM domains should mimic cadherin in producing a defined structure (staple) that will reversibly adhere intracellular membranes when it faces the cytoplasm, or in the present application produce intra-lumenal adhesions within Golgi cisternae when the FM repeats are lumenally-oriented.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference based on the known properties of cadherins and FM domains.

claim: CD8lumenal is a chimeric protein designed as the basic unit of a lumenal membrane staple.
source_text: As the basic unit of a lumenal membrane staple we designed a chimeric protein, termed CD8
evidence_reasoning: This describes the experimental design and construction of the key reagent.

claim: When CD8lumenal is expressed in HeLa cells in the absence of disaggregating drug, discrete electron-dense plaques are readily observed by electron microscopy.
source_text: When CD8lumenal is expressed in HeLa cells in the absence of the disaggregating drug AP21998, numerous, discrete electron-dense plaques are in fact readily observed by electron microscopy (Figure 1B, red square).
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from electron microscopy experiments.

claim: Lumenal staples trigger lumenal constrictions within ER tubules whose separation averages 25 ± 5 nm.
source_text: The staples trigger lumenal constrictions within ER tubules (Figure 1C) whose separation averages 25 ± 5 nm
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data.

claim: Cytosolic staples that harbor FM domains at the cytosolic face of membranes cause ER membranes to be artificially stacked.
source_text: Remarkably, when we used cytosolic staples that harbor the FM domains at the cytosolic face of the membranes (CD8cytosolic), ER membranes were artificially stacked, confirming the trans–nature of the staples interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence_reasoning: This experimental result confirms the trans-interaction property of the staples.

claim: The artificial stacking of ER membranes by cytosolic staples confirms the trans-nature of the staples interaction.
source_text: Remarkably, when we used cytosolic staples that harbor the FM domains at the cytosolic face of the membranes (CD8cytosolic), ER membranes were artificially stacked, confirming the trans–nature of the staples interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence_reasoning: The trans-interaction is inferred from the observed membrane stacking behavior.

claim: Staples resulting from trans-interactions (two opposed membranes) were exclusively visualized, though cis-interactions on the same membrane cannot be ruled out when physical constraints are favorable.
source_text: Although we exclusively visualized staples resulting from trans-interactions (two opposed membranes), we cannot rule out that cis-interactions (on the same membrane) may occurs when the physical constraints are favorable.
evidence_reasoning: The observation is data-driven, but the possibility of cis-interactions is speculative.

claim: At the confocal level, staples show a reticular pattern typical of ER.
source_text: At the confocal level, the staples showed a reticular pattern typical of ER.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from confocal microscopy.

claim: When AP21998 is added to disaggregate the staples in the ER, CD8lumenal is transported to the plasma membrane.
source_text: Only when AP21998 is added to disaggregate the staples in the ER is CD8
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by multiple experimental approaches including surface labeling and biochemical assays.

claim: Treatment with disaggregating drug for 4 hours increases TritonX-100 solubility of CD8lumenal.
source_text: When tested by SDS-PAGE, the disaggregating drug increased Triton-X100 solubility (without sonication procedure) of CD8
evidence_reasoning: This is a biochemical measurement showing changes in protein solubility.

claim: Disaggregated CD8lumenal shows reduced mobility on SDS-PAGE gel.
source_text: Disaggregated-CD8lumenal shows reduced mobility on SDS-PAGE gel (* upper band).
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from gel electrophoresis experiments.

claim: Jacalin, a lectin that binds galactose residues, exclusively precipitates disaggregated CD8lumenal.
source_text: Jacalin, a lectin that binds galactose residues, exclusively precipitates disaggregated CD8lumenal.
evidence_reasoning: This is a biochemical result from lectin precipitation experiments.

claim: The reduced mobility and Jacalin precipitation of disaggregated CD8lumenal indicate that it is glycosylated in the Golgi.
source_text: When tested by SDS-PAGE, the disaggregating drug increased Triton-X100 solubility (without sonication procedure) of CD8... Disaggregated-CD8lumenal shows reduced mobility on SDS-PAGE gel (* upper band)... Jacalin, a lectin that binds galactose residues, exclusively precipitates disaggregated CD8lumenal.
evidence_reasoning: The combination of reduced mobility and lectin binding is interpreted as evidence of glycosylation, which occurs in the Golgi.

claim: ER-aggregated CD8lumenal forms staples that remain within the ER during their lifetime.
source_text: Together, these results showed that ER-aggregated CD8lumenal forms staples that remain within the ER during their lifetime.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is supported by multiple imaging and biochemical experiments.

claim: Adding disaggregating drug dissolves a portion of the ER staples and allows disaggregated CD8lumenal to behave as a proper anterograde cargo.
source_text: However, this is a reversible state because adding the disaggregating drug dissolved a portion of the staples and allowed disaggregated CD8lumenal to behave as a proper anterograde cargo that is glycosylated in the Golgi prior to being targeted to the cell surface membrane.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by experiments showing transport and glycosylation upon drug addition.

claim: A 20°C temperature block slows exit from the trans-most Golgi cisterna (TGN) more than it slows ER to Golgi transport or transport from cis to trans Golgi.
source_text: A classic example is the 20°C temperature block, which slows exit from the trans-most Golgi cisterna (TGN) more than it slows ER → Golgi transport or transport from cis → trans Golgi (Matlin and Simons, 1983).
evidence_reasoning: This is established methodology in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Temperature blocks in the 15-18°C range slow export of secretory cargo from the ER but slow anterograde transport in the Golgi stack even more, resulting in accumulation in the ERGIC and cis-most Golgi cisterna.
source_text: Temperature blocks in the 15–18°C range slow export of secretory cargo from the ER, but slow anterograde transport in the Golgi stack even more, resulting in limited penetration of the Golgi stack with accumulation in the ER–Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) and the cis-most Golgi cisterna or two (Hobman et al., 1992; Balch et al., 1994; Volchuk et al., 2000).
evidence_reasoning: This is established methodology supported by multiple citations.

claim: A 16°C temperature block was used to load and accumulate disaggregated CD8lumenal into the cis-Golgi of HeLa cells.
source_text: Following an established procedure (Volchuk et al., 2000) we employed a 16°C temperature block to load and accumulate some of the disaggregated CD8lumenal into the cis-Golgi of HeLa cells.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the experimental procedure used to position proteins in specific Golgi compartments.

claim: A portion of disaggregated CD8lumenal is precipitated by Helix Pomatia at 16°C, indicating it has reached the cis-Golgi.
source_text: An independent, biochemical test confirmed that the unassembled CD8lumenal had reached the cis-Golgi but not the trans-Golgi at 16°C. Specifically, a portion of disaggregated CD8lumenal is precipitated by Helix Pomatia (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), a lectin that binds a N-Acetyl-Galactosamine residue that is only added within the cis-Golgi (Roth et al., 1994).
evidence_reasoning: Lectin precipitation provides biochemical evidence of cis-Golgi localization, based on known glycosylation patterns.

claim: Jacalin did not precipitate CD8lumenal at 16°C, indicating it had not reached the trans-Golgi.
source_text: In contrast, the lectin Jacalin, which requires trans-Golgi localized modifications for binding (Spicer and Schulte, 1992), did not precipitate CD8lumenal at 16°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), although it did at 37°C (Figure 2D).
evidence_reasoning: The absence of Jacalin binding indicates lack of trans-Golgi modifications, confirming cis-Golgi localization.

claim: CD8lumenal re-aggregated in the Golgi at 16°C did not reach the cell surface and was retained in the Golgi.
source_text: Surprisingly, the CD8lumenal re-aggregated in the Golgi at 16°C did not reach the surface and was retained in the Golgi as judged by confocal microscopy (Figure 3B,C, lane 2).
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation and immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: Golgi retention of staples is due to controlled aggregation, because adding the drug back removes the transport block.
source_text: Golgi retention of the staples is due to controlled aggregation, because this block to transport was removed when the drug was added back, and CD8lumenal (disaggregated) now moves from the Golgi to the plasma membrane (Figure 3B,C, lane 3).
evidence_reasoning: The reversibility of the retention upon drug addition demonstrates that aggregation is the cause of retention.

claim: Cis- and trans-Golgi fluorescent markers (Grasp65 and Golgin97) can be well discriminated by confocal microscopy.
source_text: We confirmed that co-expressed cis- and trans-Golgi fluorescent markers (Grasp65 and Golgin97, respectively) could be well discriminated by confocal microscopy and the degree of separation quantified with Pearson's coefficient
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by confocal imaging and quantitative colocalization analysis.

claim: Golgi-re-aggregated CD8lumenal shows better co-localization with Grasp65 (cis-Golgi marker) than with Golgin97 (trans-Golgi marker).
source_text: Confocal micrograph showed that Golgi-re-aggregated-CD8lumenal, presumably forming cis-Golgi lumenal staples, showed a better co-localization with Grasp65 (3) than with Golgin97 (2).
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy and Pearson's coefficient analysis.

claim: Staples are recognized in thin sections as electron dense plaques within Golgi cisternae.
source_text: The staples were recognized in thin sections as electron dense plaques within Golgi cisternae (arrows,
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from electron microscopy.

claim: Staples remain at one face of the Golgi within the first cistern or first two cisternae after 2 or 6 hour chase at 20°C.
source_text: Electron-micrograph showing that the staples (white arrows) remain at one face of the Golgi, within the first cistern (A) or in the first two cisternae (B and C) after 2 or 6 hr chase at 20°C, respectively.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy at multiple time points.

claim: Staples that form flat features are localized at the center of the cisternae, and their topological arrangements prevent them from localizing at the rim of the cisternae.
source_text: Staples that form flat features are localized at the center of the cisternae. Their topological arrangements prevent them from localizing at the rim of the cisternae.
evidence_reasoning: The central localization is observed, and the exclusion from rims is inferred from the structural constraints of the staples.

claim: Clathrin, which labels the trans-Golgi, and staples are at two opposite faces of the Golgi.
source_text: Electron-micrograph showing clathrin (10 nm gold particle), which label the trans-Golgi, and the staples (5 nm gold particles) are at two opposite faces of the Golgi.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by immuno-electron microscopy with dual labeling.

claim: Gm130, a cis Golgi marker, is at the same face as the staples.
source_text: Gm130 (5 nm gold particles), a cis Golgi marker, is at the same face as the staples (10 nm gold particles).
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by immuno-electron microscopy with dual labeling.

claim: Staples formed at 20°C do not reach the plasma membrane.
source_text: Immunoblot, after surface biotinylation, showing that the staples formed in the medial/trans Golgi do not reach the PM.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation experiments.

claim: Staples formed at 20°C are retained throughout the Golgi and not only at the TGN face.
source_text: Electron micrograph showing that the staples formed at 20°C are actually retained throughout the Golgi and not only at the TGN face.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy showing staple distribution.

claim: Staples formed at 16°C and chased at 20°C harbor a cis-glycan signature but not the trans-glycan signature.
source_text: Consistently, lectin-precipitation experiment showed that staples formed at 16°C and chased at 20°C harbored a cis-glycan signature (precipitated by Helix pomatis) but not the trans-glycan signature (not precipitated by Jacalin)
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by lectin precipitation experiments showing differential glycosylation patterns.

claim: Membrane staples formed in the first cisterna of the Golgi stack do not move across the stack, even after several hours.
source_text: Altogether, the above experiments reveal that membrane staples formed in the first cisterna of the Golgi stack do not move across the stack, even after several hours.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is supported by multiple experimental approaches including EM, confocal microscopy, and biochemical assays.

claim: Staples accumulate at the central portion of the cis-most cisternae being excluded from their rims.
source_text: Interestingly, the staples accumulate at the central portion of the cis-most cisternae (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) being excluded from their rims.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from electron microscopy.

claim: The exclusion of staples from rims could be the consequence of the fixed dimension of the staples, which are too small to fit across a dilated rim.
source_text: This could be the consequence of the fixed dimension of the staples, which are too small to fit across a dilated rim (Figure 5D).
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference based on the structural constraints of staples and rim dimensions.

claim: Staples would be expected to preferentially form in the flattened central regions of a cisterna.
source_text: So, the staples would be expected to preferentially form in the flattened central regions of a cisterna.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the dimensional constraints and observed localization patterns.

claim: Staples deposited in later Golgi cisternae are also static.
source_text: We therefore wanted to see if staples deposited in later Golgi cisternae might also be static... Surface biotinylation established that staples formed at 20°C remained at the Golgi even after the cells were warmed up to 37°C for 2 hr (Figure 5G), similar to the cis-Golgi staples.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation experiments with staples formed at different Golgi levels.

claim: Staples formed at 20°C were present and retained throughout the entire Golgi stack, including the trans-most Golgi cisterna.
source_text: Electron microscopy revealed that the staples formed at 20°C were present and retained throughout the entire Golgi stack, including the trans-most Golgi cisterna (Figure 5H).
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy showing staple distribution throughout the stack.

claim: The retention of staples at every level of the Golgi stack emphasizes the static nature of the cisterna on the time scale being studied (5-6 hours).
source_text: The fact that the staples are retained in place at every level of the Golgi stack further emphasizes the static nature of the cisterna on the time scale being studied (5–6 hr)
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from the comprehensive observation of staple retention at all Golgi levels.

claim: The stable cis localization of staples at 16°C does not result from anterograde transport followed by efficient retrieval to the cis cisternae.
source_text: and also rules out the caveat that the apparently stable cis localization of staples at 16°C results from anterograde transport followed by efficient retrieval to the cis cisternae.
evidence_reasoning: The retention of staples at all levels rules out a retrieval mechanism as an explanation.

claim: VSVG-GFP is targeted to the plasma membrane regardless of the re-aggregation status of CD8lumenal within the Golgi.
source_text: Immunoblot, after surface biotinylation, showing that VSVG-GFP is targeted to the PM regardless of the re-aggregation status of CD8lumenal within the Golgi.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by surface biotinylation experiments showing VSVG transport in the presence of staples.

claim: The rate of release of PA-GFP-VSV-G from long-term (4 hour) stapled Golgi is indistinguishable from that measured from a non-stapled Golgi.
source_text: The rate of the release (half-time ∼ 5 min) of PA-GFP-VSV-G from even long-term (4 hr) stapled Golgi was indistinguishable from that measured from a non-stapled Golgi identified with a red-tagged Golgi marker (ST-RFP) (Figure 6B).
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by photoactivation experiments measuring transport kinetics.

claim: Stapled-Golgi remains properly stacked and is fully functional for transport.
source_text: This observation and the fact that stapled-Golgi remain properly stacked established that stapled-Golgi is fully functional for transport.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from the combination of structural integrity and functional transport measurements.

claim: Cells harboring stapled-Golgi for 2 hours show 92.5 ± 13% of freshly secreted collagen-I when compared to cells harboring normal Golgi.
source_text: Cells harboring stapled-Golgi for 2 hr showed 92.5 ± 13% of freshly secreted collagen-I when compared to cells harboring normal Golgi (set to 100%).
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement of collagen secretion in the presence of staples.

claim: Anterograde transport of Collagen-I is not altered when staples are positioned within the Golgi.
source_text: This suggests that, as reported above with for VSV-G, anterograde transport of Collagen-I is not altered when staples are positioned within the Golgi.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from the quantitative secretion measurements showing minimal difference.

claim: The kinetics of secretion for collagen-I and MMP2 do not show robust differences whether the Golgi apparatus is stapled or not.
source_text: The kinetics of secretion for both proteins did not show any robust differences whether the Golgi apparatus was stapled or not (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by time-course experiments measuring secretion rates.

claim: Redistribution of Golgi enzymes into the ER under BFA treatment was observed whether Golgi staples were present or not.
source_text: Redistribution of Golgi enzymes into the ER was observed whether Golgi staples were present or not (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy showing BFA-induced redistribution.

claim: Staples localized either within the Golgi or within the ER readily diffuse within the cisternal membranes.
source_text: FRAP experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) showed that staples (localized either within the Golgi or within the ER) readily diffuse within the cisternal membranes
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments measuring fluorescence recovery.

claim: Staples do not perturb the diffusion of Golgi resident enzymes.
source_text: FRAP experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) showed that staples (localized either within the Golgi or within the ER) readily diffuse within the cisternal membranes and do not perturb the diffusion of Golgi resident enzymes
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments comparing diffusion rates.

claim: Golgi-staples diffuse only slightly more slowly than disaggregated CD8lumenal at 20°C.
source_text: in fact, Golgi-staples diffused only slightly more slowly than disaggregated CD8lumenal at 20°C (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative comparison from FRAP experiments.

claim: The normal diffusion of staples explains why essential functions of the Golgi such as transport and glycosylation are not perturbed by their presence.
source_text: This would explain in a satisfying manner why the essential functions of the Golgi (and ER) such as transport and glycosylation are not perturbed by the presence of the staples, since these behave like any cargo or resident protein within the membrane
evidence_reasoning: This explanation is inferred from the FRAP data showing normal diffusion behavior.

claim: Soluble aggregates compositionally similar to the staples rapidly move forward through the Golgi, analogous to collagens.
source_text: Previously, we found that soluble aggregates that are compositionally similar to the staples (the main difference being that they were not membrane-anchored) rapidly move forward through the Golgi, analogous to collagens (Volchuk et al., 2000).
evidence_reasoning: This refers to previous experimental findings by the authors.

claim: Soluble aggregates are concentrated at the rims of the Golgi cisternae, analogous to collagens.
source_text: We noted that these soluble aggregates were concentrated at the rims of the Golgi cisternae, analogous to collagens.
evidence_reasoning: This is an observation from electron microscopy studies.

claim: When lumenally-expressed soluble FM4 and membrane-bound FM4 proteins are present in the ER, they are efficiently co-immunoprecipitated from cell extracts.
source_text: As expected, when the two FM-containing proteins were present in the ER they were efficiently co-immunoprecipitated from cell extracts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: When soluble and membrane-bound FM proteins are disaggregated, allowed to leave the ER, and then re-aggregated in the cis-Golgi, the Golgi-modified forms are no longer co-immunoprecipitated.
source_text: However, when these same proteins were disaggregated and allowed to leave the ER and then re-aggregated for 1 hr in the cis-Golgi at 16°C, or even further in the Golgi stack at 20°C, the Golgi-modified forms of these same proteins were no longer co-immunoprecipitated (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing lack of interaction in the Golgi.

claim: Homo-aggregates constituted of soluble cargo (hGH) are efficiently formed even after re-aggregation at 16°C or 20°C.
source_text: On the contrary homo-aggregates constituted of soluble cargo (hGH) were efficiently formed even after re-aggregation at 16°C or 20°C (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing homo-aggregation.

claim: Hetero-aggregates are not formed efficiently within the Golgi cisternae.
source_text: This suggests that hetero-aggregates are not formed efficiently within the Golgi cisternae.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data showing lack of hetero-aggregation in the Golgi.

claim: Soluble and membrane-bound FM proteins segregate into separate aggregates within the same Golgi area.
source_text: Confocal microscopy independently established that the soluble and membrane-bound FM proteins segregated into separate aggregates within the same Golgi area
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy showing spatial separation.

claim: DsRed-hGH is secreted regardless of its own re-aggregation status or the re-aggregation status of CD8lumenal.
source_text: Immunoblot, after surface biotinylation and TCA precipitation of the media, showing that DsRed-hGH is secreted regardless of its own re-aggregation status, or the re-aggregation status of CD8lumenal.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by biochemical analysis of secreted proteins.

claim: Prior to being secreted, disaggregated and re-aggregated DsRed-hGH are cleaved by furin.
source_text: Prior to being secreted disaggregated and re-aggregated DsRed-hGH are cleaved by furin.
evidence_reasoning: This is observed by the appearance of cleaved forms on immunoblots.

claim: When aggregates accumulated in the cis-Golgi are allowed to move anterograde at 20°C, approximately 75% of the staples remain at the cis-face of the Golgi, whereas approximately 75% of the soluble aggregates are transported to the opposite, trans-face of the same Golgi stacks.
source_text: When aggregates accumulated in the cis-Golgi are allowed to move anterograde through but not exit the Golgi following warm-up to 20°C, ≈75% of the staples, as expected, remain at the cis-face of the Golgi, whereas ≈75% of the soluble aggregates are transported to the opposite, trans-face of the same Golgi stacks (Figure 7B and graph).
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy analysis.

claim: The anterograde transport process permits large soluble aggregates to be carried forward between cisternae that are immobile.
source_text: We conclude that the anterograde transport process permits large soluble aggregates to be carried forward between cisternae that are immobile.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from the differential behavior of soluble aggregates versus membrane staples.

claim: Staples freely diffuse like any other membrane constituent, making it unlikely that a moderate amount would broadly perturb Golgi transport or function.
source_text: On the one hand, because staples freely diffuse like any other membrane constituent it is hard to imagine how a moderate amount of staples would broadly perturb Golgi transport or function such as glycosylation, and there is no positive evidence from our studies that they do so.
evidence_reasoning: This reasoning is based on FRAP data showing normal diffusion and functional assays showing normal transport.

claim: Staples span and link between two sides of the cisterna, explaining why they remain in the thin centers of the cisternae far from the dilated rims.
source_text: On the other hand, because they span and link between two sides of the cisterna, it is easy to see why staples should remain in the thin centers of the cisternae, far from the dilated rims (whose width is too great to accommodate the staples) where transport vesicles bud
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference based on the structural properties of staples and cisternal geometry.

claim: Staples would be sterically excluded from budding COPI or other vesicles if they occasionally reached a rim.
source_text: and also why staples would be sterically excluded from budding COPI or other vesicles if they did occasionally reach a rim, and thus would remain within the cisterna.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference based on the size and structure of staples relative to vesicle dimensions.

claim: Membrane staples localize to the central regions of Golgi cisternae where they segregate from large soluble aggregates which mainly concentrate at the dilated rims.
source_text: With this in mind, our findings can be simply summarized as follows: 1) membrane staples localize to the central regions of Golgi cisternae where they segregate from large soluble aggregates which mainly concentrate at the dilated rims
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary of multiple experimental observations from EM and confocal microscopy.

claim: Membrane staples remain in place as anterograde transport occurs, whereas large soluble aggregates and small cargo are transported at normal rates.
source_text: and 2) membrane staples remain in place as anterograde transport occurs, whereas large soluble aggregates and small cargo are transported at normal rates.
evidence_reasoning: This is a summary of the key experimental findings from multiple assays.

claim: While the cisternae in the stack are static, the rims of cisternae are mobile in the anterograde direction, a process termed 'rim progression'.
source_text: The obvious explanation of the above is that while the cisternae in the stack (containing staples mainly in their central regions) are static, the rims of cisternae—mainly containing the soluble aggregates—are mobile (at least on the average) in the anterograde direction, a process we term 'rim progression'.
evidence_reasoning: This model is proposed to explain the differential behavior of staples versus soluble aggregates.

claim: The unique nature of the artificial staples prevents definitive conclusion that 'pure maturation' does not occur in regions of the Golgi stacks depleted of staples.
source_text: However, the unique nature of the artificial staples prevents us from definitively concluding that 'pure maturation' does not occur in region of the Golgi stacks that are depleted of staples.
evidence_reasoning: This acknowledges a limitation in the interpretation due to the artificial nature of the experimental system.

claim: It is possible that staples introduced non-obvious, minor side effects on Golgi, though anterograde transport through stapled Golgi is not altered.
source_text: Although we established by using broad sets of assays that anterograde transport through stapled Golgi is not altered, we cannot rule out that staples introduced, non-obvious, minor side effects on Golgi.
evidence_reasoning: This acknowledges a potential caveat despite the lack of evidence for major perturbations.

claim: Rim progression could be easily mis-interpreted as cisternal progression if the only marker being studied is in the rim.
source_text: It would be very easy to mis-interpret rim progression as cisternal progression if the only marker being studied is in the rim (Bonfanti et al., 1998).
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about potential misinterpretation of previous studies.

claim: The principal evidence for cisternal progression in Golgi stacks was the mobility of large aggregates like collagens that are located to the rims.
source_text: In retrospect, the principal evidence for cisternal progression in Golgi stacks was the mobility of large aggregates like collagens that are located to the rims (Bonfanti et al., 1998).
evidence_reasoning: This summarizes the key evidence from previous literature supporting cisternal progression.

claim: A stricter interpretation of collagen data would conclude that at least some portions of the cisterna containing collagen aggregates (the rims) are mobile, without reaching conclusions about the rest of the cisterna.
source_text: But in retrospect a stricter interpretation of that data would have been to conclude that the 'at least some portions' of the cisterna containing the collagen aggregates (i.e., the rims) are mobile, without reaching any conclusion with respect to the rest of the cisterna.
evidence_reasoning: This is a reinterpretation of previous data in light of the current findings.

claim: While the majority of collagen aggregates are rapidly transported, a sizable minority (approximately 20%) remains in the Golgi cisternae, mainly in the centers of the cisternae.
source_text: A striking feature of the collagen data is that while the majority of the aggregates are indeed rapidly transported, a sizable minority (∼20% [Bonfanti et al., 1998]) remains in the Golgi cisternae, mainly in the centers of the cisternae, consistent with our results and interpretation.
evidence_reasoning: This observation from previous literature is consistent with the current findings.

claim: The most likely mechanism for rim progression would be cycles of fission and fusion that are known to take place in the Golgi.
source_text: We do not know how the rims of otherwise stable stacks progress, but the most likely possibility would be cycles of fission and fusion that are known to take place in the Golgi (Pfeffer, 2010).
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative mechanism based on known Golgi dynamics from the literature.

claim: Rab cascades could organize rim progression in the cis to trans direction according to the Cisternal Progenitor model.
source_text: Pfeffer has considered how this could be organized in the cis → trans direction by known Rab cascades in the Cisternal Progenitor model, which could well be the basis for the transport of rims dilated with aggregates.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative mechanism based on Pfeffer's theoretical model.

claim: After fission, a transiently separated rim would remain in register in the stack because its membrane would still be engaged in stacking/tethering interactions.
source_text: We would imagine that after fission a transiently separated rim would nonetheless remain in register in the stack because its membrane would still be engaged in stacking/tethering interactions.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative explanation for how rim progression could maintain Golgi organization.

claim: Pulse-chase experiments showed the appearance of detached rims closely-associated with the edges of the stack that transiently appeared during the transport of soluble aggregates.
source_text: Pulse-chase experiments (Volchuk et al., 2000) showed the appearance of detached rims closely-associated with the edges of the stack that transiently appeared during the transport of soluble aggregates (which we termed mega-vesicles at the time).
evidence_reasoning: This refers to previous experimental observations by the authors.

claim: To the extent that the bulk of a Golgi stack is static on the time scale of anterograde transport, this reduces the quantitative demand on retrograde transport of Golgi resident proteins and the need for cisternal maturation.
source_text: To the extent that the bulk of a Golgi stack is static on the time scale of anterograde transport, this reduces the quantitative demand on retrograde transport of Golgi resident proteins and the need for cisternal maturation.
evidence_reasoning: This is a logical inference about the implications of static cisternae for Golgi homeostasis.

claim: In budding yeast, where cisternae generally do not stack, the process of cisternal maturation is well documented.
source_text: In budding yeast, where cisternae generally do not stack, the process of cisternal maturation is well documented, though formal proof that anterograde cargo is present in maturing cisternae is still lacking (Losev et al., 2006; Matsuura-Tokita et al., 2006).
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about yeast Golgi organization, supported by citations.

claim: Cisternal maturation may be important in re-assembly of the Golgi after cell division.
source_text: We do not wish to conclude that cisternal maturation does not occur in the stacked Golgi of complex plants and animals, or that it may not be important in re-assembly of the Golgi after cell division
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative statement about potential roles of cisternal maturation.

claim: Cisternal maturation does not appear to be required on the time scale of biosynthetic protein transport in interphase in stacked Golgi.
source_text: only that it does not appear to be required on the time scale of biosynthetic protein transport in interphase in stacked Golgi.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental findings showing static cisternae during active transport.

claim: Rim progression is dedicated to large soluble aggregates that due to physical constraints are forced into the rims away from adhesive centers of cisternae.
source_text: We propose that rim progression is dedicated to large soluble aggregates that due to physical constraints are forced into the rims away from adhesive centers of cisternae, and differs mechanistically from vesicle budding.
evidence_reasoning: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed spatial segregation and differential transport.

claim: COPI vesicles bud extensively from the rims of Golgi cisternae at every level and contain both retrograde-directed cargo and anterograde-directed cargo such as insulin, albumin, and VSV-G.
source_text: COPI vesicles are known to bud extensively from the rims of Golgi cisternae at every level and contain–in addition to retrograde-directed cargo–anterograde-directed cargo such as insulin, albumin, and VSV-G (Rothman, 2010)
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about COPI vesicle function, supported by citation.

claim: COPI vesicle budding appears to be the principal pathway for transport of smaller cargoes across static cisternae.
source_text: so this biochemically well-understood pathway (Popoff et al., 2011) would seem to be the principal contender.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred as the most likely mechanism based on known COPI function and the current findings.

claim: There may be other parallel pathways for cargo transport depending on physiological state, specifically budding/fusing tubules, which have been observed especially under conditions of protein over-expression.
source_text: There may well be other, parallel pathways depending on physiological state, specifically budding/fusing tubules, which have been observed especially under conditions of protein over-expression (Ladinsky et al., 1999; Trucco et al., 2004).
evidence_reasoning: This acknowledges alternative mechanisms observed in the literature, with speculation about their physiological relevance.

claim: The Golgi cisternae can be divided into two functionally distinct domains: the centers and the rims.
source_text: Our findings, along with other evidence (Brugger et al., 2000; Patterson et al., 2008), point to a broad division of the Golgi cisternae into two functionally distinct domains: the centers and the rims.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conceptual model supported by the current findings and previous literature.

claim: The rims specialize in exit and entry into the stack and are dynamic, while the centers are static and adherent to form the stack and specialize in biosynthesis and processing.
source_text: The rims specialize in exit and entry into the stack and are dynamic, while the centers are static and adherent to form the stack and specialize in biosynthesis and processing.
evidence_reasoning: This functional division is inferred from the differential behavior and localization of different cargo types.
